claims.text: Pristine equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Heating HfNbTaTiZr induces a transient phase transformation.
The transient transformation creates short-range ordered clusters.
Differential thermal expansion among the constituent elements creates local thermal stresses during heating.
Local thermal stresses promote the formation of ordered clusters.
Transient ordered clusters modify dislocation mobility.
Modification of dislocation mobility by the clusters increases creep resistance.
Transient structural inhomogeneities alter the alloy's thermoelastic response and elastic moduli.
Transient structural inhomogeneities explain the microhardness changes associated with cold rolling.
Thermally cycled specimens will have different creep rates from isothermally held specimens.
Thermally cycled specimens will likely have lower high-temperature creep rates than isothermally held specimens.
Thermal cycling will alter elastic moduli relative to an isothermal baseline.
Thermal cycling will change microhardness relative to an isothermal baseline.
The predicted mechanical-property differences will correlate with the presence of short-range order.
The effects of transient ordering will be most pronounced between 600 and 1250 °C.
The transient ordered state exists only from 600 to 1250 °C.
At room temperature or outside 600–1250 °C, the alloy returns to a homogenized, disordered state.
Isothermally held baseline samples exhibit steady mechanical and elastic responses without transient ordering.
Transient superlattice reflections or peak splitting in XRD would indicate short-range order.

contradictions.description: The proposal anticipates assessing post-treatment room-temperature mechanical changes, but the boundary states that at room temperature the alloy reverts to the homogenized, disordered baseline state. It does not explain how ordering-correlated room-temperature differences could persist after the proposed mediator has disappeared.
